data.hook: Two years into Donald Trump's second term, polls show only 17% of Americans believe kids will have it better than their parents—a stark sign of economic unease.
data.name: Debate Intensifies Over Trump's Affordability Crisis Claims
data.summary: Social media users fiercely debate whether high costs for gas, groceries, and housing stem from Trump policies like tariffs or lingering Biden-era inflation. Trump counters that his administration inherited the problem and has lowered prices through tax cuts and energy boosts, while critics blame him for ongoing 3.7% inflation above Fed targets. Midterm losses handed Democrats House and Senate control, driven by voter frustration over living costs as the top issue.

data.hook: House Democrats pledged lower costs and an end to foreign wars, but a stark graphic of soaring prices under the prior administration drew swift pushback from skeptics.
data.name: House Democrats Promise Lower Costs and Peace Amid Price Rise Backlash
data.summary: Democrats highlighted Republican chaos while promising affordable healthcare and lower costs, alongside claims that they would end what they called Donald Trump's 265-day war with Iran. A Fox Business graphic detailed sharp increases from January 2021 to May 2024, including 20.1% overall inflation, 35.3% home prices, 148% mortgage rates, 46% gas, and 21.5% food prices—figures backed by Bureau of Labor Statistics and USDA data. Critics replied by tying the promises to past Democratic records on inflation, borders, and foreign funding, questioning their credibility in the heated exchange.

data.name: Americans Split on Affordability Crisis Amid Rising Inflation
data.summary: President Trump blames high prices on the prior Biden administration, claiming they are now way down, while supporters argue an information operation misled voters on affordability. Critics point to Trump's tariffs and the ongoing Iran conflict, which spiked energy prices with gasoline up 9.1% in September as inflation hit 3.7%. A post-election survey showed voters more likely to blame tariffs than the war itself, reflecting divided views on groceries, energy, and housing costs.

data.hook: Texas Senator John Cornyn shared a New York Times piece celebrating the state's Democratic shift, right after major election losses for Republicans.
data.name: Cornyn Faces Conservative Backlash for Sharing Texas 'Bluer' Article
data.summary: In the wake of November 2026 elections where Democrats flipped Texas's U.S. Senate seat, governor's office, and other key positions, Cornyn posted a Times article titled 'Whatever You Thought Texas Was, It’s Bigger and Bluer Than That.' Conservatives online quickly called it petty, labeling him a sore loser after his earlier losses: a 2026 primary defeat to Ken Paxton and a failed 2024 bid for Senate Republican leader against John Thune. The backlash highlighted growing questions about Cornyn's ties to the Texas GOP base as his term ends, even as he continues work like co-chairing the Senate India Caucus.

data.hook: At a White House briefing, President Trump stood firm with charts showing public backing for deportations, pushing back against amnesty ideas from reporters.
data.name: Trump Reaffirms Deportation Stance Amid Poll Support
data.summary: Trump rejected broad legal status for 20 to 30 million illegal immigrants, declaring 'WE’RE NOT gonna let immigration destroy our country' while noting Hispanic support for deportations and border security. A new YouGov poll found 51 percent of Americans favor deporting most illegal immigrants, with only 7 percent wanting all to stay, though older surveys show support for limited paths for long-term residents. Officials like JD Vance criticized amnesty calls, and the administration appointed Stephen Miller as chief of staff, signaling focus on criminals and border enforcement despite some flexibility on DACA.

data.hook: Fresh off strong midterm victories, Democrats are rallying behind Sen. Chris Van Hollen to replace Chuck Schumer as Senate majority leader.
data.name: Democrats Push Van Hollen for Senate Majority Leader After Midterm Wins
data.summary: Van Hollen announced his challenge on Nov. 12, calling for new leadership to answer voters who rejected the status quo. Strategist David Axelrod urged Schumer to serve as a two-year bridge, drawing a lesson from Joe Biden's midterm misstep. With endorsements from Bernie Sanders and a poll showing Democratic voters favoring change, the caucus faces a secret-ballot vote on Dec. 1 that will shape the new Congress.

data.hook: With just 44 days left before Democrats take the Senate majority, Speaker Mike Johnson is calling every Republican back to Washington—except for serious medical issues—to push through key bills.
data.name: GOP Tensions Rise as Congress Nears End with Johnson Urging Attendance
data.summary: Johnson's November 20 letter highlights the House passing over 1,000 measures while Senate Democrats blocked nearly 700, stressing the need to advance government funding, the NDAA, and more before January. Conservatives are voicing frustration at Senate Majority Leader John Thune, with President Trump blaming him for stalling military funding and air traffic control reforms, and a White House official citing a held-up $350 billion Pentagon boost. Meanwhile, Rep. Tim Burchett announced his 2028 Senate run in Tennessee, polling strongly and drawing cheers as a conservative fighter. These moves underscore Republican pressure to act aggressively in their final weeks of unified control.

data.hook: In his final weeks as a senator, Thom Tillis is drawing fire from fellow conservatives for a bill they say hands Democrats a win by crippling lawsuits against banks.
data.name: Conservatives Blast Sen. Tillis Over Litigation Funding Tax Bill
data.summary: The Tackling Predatory Litigation Funding Act would slap a 40.8% excise tax on third-party lawsuit financing, which critics like former Justice official Chad Mizelle argue would gut funding for conservative legal battles over debanking by big banks. Figures such as Laura Ingraham and Riley Gaines voiced frustration, with Gaines stressing the need for tools to hold banks accountable, while North Carolina locals called Tillis an embarrassment. Tillis defends the bill as curbing abusive practices and has backed separate anti-debanking measures, but the backlash has Republicans urging leadership to block it before year's end amid his lame-duck retirement.

data.hook: Young men who powered Trump's 2024 win largely stayed home or backed Democrats in the 2026 midterms, driving a Democratic surge across states.
data.name: Young Trump Voters Swing to Democrats in 2026 Midterms
data.summary: Post-election analysis shows that of every 100 Trump 2024 voters, 63 voted Republican, 4 switched to Democrats, and 33 stayed home—while Harris voters turned out at 85% for Democrats. Young men ages 18-29 led the shift, moving left in every state's House races and key Senate contests, with non-college men swinging 64-77 points against Republicans in Texas, South Carolina, and Mississippi. Republicans highlight turnout drops among young, non-college, Hispanic, and rural voters as the key factor, amid economic pressures like higher gas prices. Both parties see these fluid voters as up for grabs in future races.

data.hook: Even after the midterms, a new poll reveals steady public support for tougher immigration enforcement, with sharp divides across party lines.
data.name: Poll Shows 51% of Americans Back Deporting Most Illegal Immigrants
data.summary: A fresh Economist/YouGov survey of 1,628 U.S. adults from November 13-16 found 51% favor deporting all or most people who entered illegally, including 23% wanting everyone gone immediately and 28% allowing exceptions for those married to Americans or long-term residents without records. Support splits sharply: 83% of Republicans back it, while 41% overall prefer limiting deportations to serious criminals and independents nearly even at 47% for broad action. The results challenge claims of shifting voter views and highlight ongoing debates over enforcement amid political promises like amnesty.
